title: Database Sharding
description: Learn horizontal partitioning techniques, sharding strategies, and trade-offs for scaling databases beyond a single machine.

data.text: Sharding splits a large database into smaller, independent pieces called shards. Each shard lives on a separate server and handles a subset of the total data and traffic. Sharding lets you scale horizontally when vertical scaling—buying a bigger server—hits cost or performance limits. It is one of the most important database scale-out techniques in system design.

A single database server eventually runs out of CPU, memory, disk I/O, or network bandwidth. Even with the best hardware, there is a practical ceiling. Sharding distributes the load across multiple commodity servers, letting the system grow by adding more machines. The downside is operational complexity: queries, transactions, and schema changes must span multiple shards.

The sharding key determines how data is distributed. Horizontal sharding by range stores consecutive key ranges on the same shard, which is simple but can create hot spots if users are clustered by creation date. Hash-based sharding applies a hash function to the sharding key, distributing data evenly but making range queries expensive. Directory-based sharding uses a lookup table, offering flexibility at the cost of a single point of failure.

data.title: Hash-based sharding logic
data.content: Hash the user ID to route each user to a shard:
data.code:
-- Pseudocode for shard routing
function getShard(userId, shardCount):
  hash = crc32(userId)
  return hash % shardCount

-- With 4 shards:
-- user_id 101 -> shard 1
-- user_id 205 -> shard 2
-- user_id 307 -> shard 3
-- user_id 499 -> shard 0

data.text: A hot spot occurs when one shard receives disproportionate traffic because of poor key selection. In a social network, sharding by user ID causes no hot spots, but sharding by country can overload the shard for the United States. Resharding redistributes data when you add or remove shards. It requires moving large volumes of data with minimal downtime, so choose a shard count that will not require frequent resharding.

data.caption: Shard routing and hot spot avoidance
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Client request with user_id] --> B[Shard router]
    B --> C[hash(user_id) mod N]
    C --> D[Route to shard 0]
    C --> E[Route to shard 1]
    C --> F[Route to shard 2]
    C --> G[Route to shard 3]
    D --> H[Even distribution]
    E --> H
    F --> H
    G --> H

data.text: Operations that span shards are expensive. A global COUNT query must aggregate results from every shard. Distributed transactions requiring two-phase commit across shards add latency and failure modes. In interviews, design your schema and access patterns to minimize cross-shard operations. Denormalize data or maintain aggregates when global queries are frequent.

data.title: Application-level sharding
data.text: Many systems implement sharding at the application layer rather than relying on database-managed sharding. This gives full control over routing, rebalancing, and failure handling.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Sharding distributes data and load across multiple servers to enable horizontal scale.
Hash-based sharding provides even distribution; range-based sharding simplifies range queries but risks hot spots.
Cross-shard operations are expensive—design for shard-local queries whenever possible.
Resharding is complex; over-provision shards or use virtual shards to reduce rebalancing frequency.
